courses.title: Organic Chemistry for Health Sciences
courses.description: Reaction mechanisms, stereochemistry, and the chemistry of alcohols, carbonyl compounds, acids, amines and aromatic compounds relevant to drugs and biomolecules.

topics.title: Reaction Mechanisms
topics.summary: Bond cleavage, nucleophiles and electrophiles, and substitution, addition and elimination reactions.

material.heading: Reactive species
material.body: Covalent bonds break by homolysis (each atom takes one electron, forming free radicals — e.g. in chlorination of alkanes under UV light) or heterolysis (one atom takes both electrons, forming ions — carbocations and carbanions). Nucleophiles are electron-rich species that donate an electron pair (OH−, CN−, NH3, H2O); electrophiles are electron-poor and accept an electron pair (H+, carbocations, NO2+). Carbocation stability increases from methyl < primary < secondary < tertiary because of inductive and hyperconjugation effects.
keyPoints: Nucleophile donates, electrophile accepts electron pairs

material.heading: Reaction types
material.body: SN2 reactions are single-step, bimolecular, favoured at primary carbons, and cause inversion of configuration (Walden inversion). SN1 reactions are two-step via a carbocation, favoured at tertiary carbons, and give racemisation. Elimination (E1, E2) forms alkenes, favoured by strong bulky bases and heat; Zaitsev's rule predicts the more substituted alkene. Alkenes undergo electrophilic addition; Markovnikov's rule states that H adds to the carbon already bearing more hydrogens. Aromatic rings undergo electrophilic substitution (nitration, halogenation, Friedel–Crafts).
keyPoints: SN2: one step, inversion, primary carbons
Markovnikov: H to the carbon with more H

questions.stem: Homolytic cleavage of a covalent bond produces:
questions.explanation: Each fragment keeps one electron, forming radicals.

questions.stem: Which is a nucleophile?
questions.explanation: Hydroxide donates an electron pair.

questions.stem: The most stable carbocation is:
questions.explanation: Alkyl groups stabilise the positive charge by induction and hyperconjugation.

questions.stem: An SN2 reaction at a chiral carbon results in:
questions.explanation: Backside attack inverts the configuration.

questions.stem: SN1 reactions proceed through a:
questions.explanation: The rate-determining step forms a carbocation.

questions.stem: When HBr adds to propene, the major product is 2-bromopropane according to:
questions.explanation: H adds to the carbon with more H atoms.

questions.stem: Aromatic compounds such as benzene typically undergo:
questions.explanation: Substitution preserves aromatic stability.

questions.stem: According to Zaitsev's rule, elimination gives mainly the:
questions.explanation: More substituted alkenes are more stable.

topics.title: Stereochemistry and Drug Action
topics.summary: Chirality, enantiomers, R/S nomenclature, geometric isomerism and their pharmaceutical importance.

material.heading: Chirality
material.body: A chiral molecule is non-superimposable on its mirror image, usually because of a carbon bearing four different groups (a stereocentre). The two mirror-image forms are enantiomers: they have identical physical properties except the direction in which they rotate plane-polarised light (dextrorotatory + / laevorotatory −). A 50:50 mixture is a racemic mixture (optically inactive). Diastereomers are stereoisomers that are not mirror images and have different physical properties. Meso compounds have stereocentres but an internal plane of symmetry, so they are achiral. Absolute configuration is assigned R or S using Cahn–Ingold–Prelog priority rules.
keyPoints: Enantiomers rotate light in opposite directions

material.heading: Importance in pharmacy
material.body: Receptors and enzymes are chiral, so enantiomers can differ in potency or toxicity. The (R)-enantiomer of thalidomide is sedative while (S)-thalidomide is teratogenic (and they interconvert in the body). S-(−)-propranolol is the active β-blocker; escitalopram is the active S-enantiomer of citalopram; levodopa (L-DOPA) is used in Parkinson's disease rather than D-DOPA. Geometric (cis–trans / E–Z) isomers arise around double bonds or rings; e.g. cisplatin is active while transplatin is not.
keyPoints: Escitalopram and levodopa are single enantiomers

questions.stem: A carbon atom attached to four different groups is called a:
questions.explanation: It gives rise to non-superimposable mirror images.

questions.stem: Enantiomers differ in their:
options: Direction of rotation of plane-polarised light
questions.explanation: They rotate light equally but in opposite directions.

questions.stem: An equimolar mixture of two enantiomers is called:
questions.explanation: A racemate shows no net optical rotation.

questions.stem: Stereoisomers that are not mirror images of each other are:
questions.explanation: Diastereomers have different physical properties.

questions.stem: Which drug disaster highlighted the importance of stereochemistry?
questions.explanation: One thalidomide enantiomer is teratogenic.

questions.stem: The R/S system of naming configuration is based on:
questions.explanation: Groups are ranked by atomic number.

questions.stem: Levodopa used in Parkinson's disease is the ___ isomer.
questions.explanation: L-DOPA crosses into the brain and is converted to dopamine.

questions.stem: Cisplatin, an anticancer drug, is active while its trans isomer is inactive. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Cis–trans isomers differ in spatial arrangement around a centre.

topics.title: Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
topics.summary: Classification, properties and reactions of alcohols, phenols and ethers.

material.heading: Alcohols
material.body: Alcohols (R–OH) are primary, secondary or tertiary depending on the number of carbons attached to the carbinol carbon. Hydrogen bonding gives them higher boiling points than alkanes of similar mass. Oxidation: primary alcohols → aldehydes → carboxylic acids; secondary → ketones; tertiary resist oxidation (the basis of the dichromate breathalyser and Lucas test differences). Ethanol is metabolised by alcohol dehydrogenase to acetaldehyde, then to acetic acid; methanol is metabolised to formaldehyde and formic acid, causing blindness and acidosis (treated with fomepizole or ethanol).

material.heading: Phenols and ethers
material.body: Phenols have –OH attached directly to a benzene ring; they are more acidic than alcohols because the phenoxide ion is resonance-stabilised, and they give a violet colour with neutral ferric chloride. Phenol (carbolic acid) was Lister's antiseptic; derivatives include cresols and chloroxylenol (Dettol). Ethers (R–O–R′) are relatively unreactive; diethyl ether was an early general anaesthetic, and modern volatile anaesthetics (isoflurane, sevoflurane) are halogenated ethers.
keyPoints: Phenols are more acidic than alcohols

questions.stem: Oxidation of a secondary alcohol gives a/an:
questions.explanation: Secondary alcohols oxidise to ketones.

questions.stem: Which alcohol resists oxidation by acidified dichromate?
questions.explanation: Tertiary alcohols lack an H on the carbinol carbon.

questions.stem: Methanol poisoning causes blindness mainly due to formation of:
questions.explanation: Formate damages the optic nerve and causes acidosis.

questions.stem: Phenols are more acidic than alcohols because:
questions.explanation: Delocalisation of the negative charge stabilises the phenoxide.

questions.stem: The test giving a violet colour with phenols is the:
questions.explanation: Phenols form coloured complexes with Fe3+.

questions.stem: Sevoflurane, an inhalational anaesthetic, is chemically a:
questions.explanation: Modern volatile anaesthetics are halogenated ethers.

questions.stem: Alcohols have higher boiling points than alkanes of similar mass because of:
questions.explanation: The –OH group forms intermolecular hydrogen bonds.

questions.stem: Ethanol is first metabolised in the liver to:
questions.explanation: Alcohol dehydrogenase converts ethanol to acetaldehyde.

topics.title: Aldehydes, Ketones, Carboxylic Acids and Esters
topics.summary: Carbonyl chemistry, identification tests, acids, esters and their hydrolysis.

material.heading: Aldehydes and ketones
material.body: The carbonyl group (C=O) is polar; its carbon is electrophilic and undergoes nucleophilic addition. Aldehydes are readily oxidised, so they reduce Tollens' reagent (silver mirror) and Fehling's/Benedict's solution (brick-red Cu2O); ketones generally do not. 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (Brady's reagent) gives orange precipitates with both. Methyl ketones and ethanol give yellow iodoform with iodine and alkali. Formaldehyde solution (formalin) is a tissue fixative; acetone is a solvent and ketone body.
keyPoints: Iodoform test: methyl ketones and ethanol

material.heading: Acids and esters
material.body: Carboxylic acids (–COOH) are weak acids, stronger when electron-withdrawing groups are nearby (trichloroacetic acid > acetic acid). They react with alcohols in acid to form esters (esterification, reversible). Esters hydrolyse in acid or base (saponification with NaOH makes soap from fats). Many drugs are esters (aspirin — acetylsalicylic acid, benzocaine) or amides (paracetamol, lidocaine); esters are generally hydrolysed faster than amides, so ester local anaesthetics have shorter action. Aspirin tablets that smell of vinegar have hydrolysed to salicylic and acetic acid.

questions.stem: Which gives a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent?
questions.explanation: Aldehydes reduce Ag+ to metallic silver.

questions.stem: The reagent that gives an orange precipitate with both aldehydes and ketones is:
questions.explanation: Brady's reagent detects the carbonyl group.

questions.stem: The typical reaction of the carbonyl group is:
questions.explanation: Nucleophiles attack the electrophilic carbonyl carbon.

questions.stem: Reaction of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol forms a/an:
questions.explanation: Esterification produces an ester and water.

questions.stem: Alkaline hydrolysis of fats to produce soap is called:
questions.explanation: NaOH hydrolyses triglycerides to glycerol and soap.

questions.stem: An old bottle of aspirin smelling of vinegar indicates hydrolysis producing:
questions.explanation: Aspirin hydrolyses to salicylic acid and acetic acid.

questions.stem: Which acid is strongest?
questions.explanation: More electron-withdrawing Cl atoms stabilise the anion.

questions.stem: The iodoform test is positive for:
questions.explanation: Ethanol is oxidised to ethanal, which gives iodoform.

topics.title: Amines, Amides and Heterocycles in Drugs
topics.summary: Basicity of amines, amide bonds, and important heterocyclic rings in medicines and biomolecules.

material.heading: Amines and amides
material.body: Amines are organic derivatives of ammonia: primary (RNH2), secondary (R2NH), tertiary (R3N) and quaternary ammonium salts (R4N+, permanently charged, e.g. neuromuscular blockers, which cannot cross the blood–brain barrier). Amines are basic because of the lone pair on nitrogen; aliphatic amines are more basic than aromatic amines like aniline (whose lone pair is delocalised into the ring). Most drugs that are weak bases form water-soluble salts (e.g. hydrochlorides). Amides (–CONH2) are very weakly basic because the lone pair is delocalised onto the carbonyl oxygen; the peptide bond is an amide bond.
keyPoints: Aliphatic amines are more basic than aniline

material.heading: Heterocycles
material.body: Heterocyclic rings contain atoms other than carbon (N, O, S). Important examples: pyridine (nicotinamide/NAD+), pyrimidine (cytosine, thymine, uracil; also in trimethoprim), purine (adenine, guanine, caffeine), imidazole (histidine; azole antifungals such as clotrimazole), indole (tryptophan, serotonin), quinoline (quinine, chloroquine), thiazole (thiamine) and the β-lactam ring (penicillins, cephalosporins). The β-lactam ring's strain explains both its antibacterial activity and its susceptibility to β-lactamases.

questions.stem: Which compound is the strongest base?
questions.explanation: Aliphatic amines are more basic than aromatic amines and amides.

questions.stem: Quaternary ammonium drugs do not cross the blood–brain barrier because they:
questions.explanation: Their permanent charge limits lipid membrane crossing.

questions.stem: Aniline is a weaker base than methylamine because:
options: Its nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the ring
questions.explanation: Resonance reduces lone-pair availability.

questions.stem: The peptide bond in proteins is chemically a/an:
questions.explanation: It links the carboxyl of one amino acid to the amine of the next.

questions.stem: Chloroquine contains which heterocyclic ring system?
questions.explanation: Chloroquine is a 4-aminoquinoline.

questions.stem: Caffeine is based on which ring system?
questions.explanation: Caffeine is a methylxanthine, a purine derivative.

questions.stem: The ring responsible for the antibacterial activity of penicillin is the:
questions.explanation: The strained β-lactam acylates penicillin-binding proteins.

questions.stem: Many basic drugs are formulated as hydrochloride salts in order to:
questions.explanation: Salts of weak bases are more water-soluble.
